walkthroughs.body_html:
Legal Moral & Ethical Issues — a core area of A-Level Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Legal Moral & Ethical Issues brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Legal Moral & Ethical Issues.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Dijkstra's algorithm fails when edges have...
options: Equal weights
Negative weights
Integer weights
Real weights

mcqs.q: What does the 'h' in A*'s f(n) = g(n) + h(n) represent?
options: History cost
Heuristic estimate to goal
Hash value
Heap depth

mcqs.q: What does in-order traversal of a binary search tree produce?
options: Only the root node.
Nodes in the order they were inserted.
OR is for numbers, XOR is for letters.
Nodes in ascending sorted order.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between OR and XOR?
options: OR is true when at least one input is true; XOR is true when exactly one input is true.
They are the same gate with different names.
OR is for numbers, XOR is for letters.
The computer crashes.

mcqs.q: What happens when 11111111 + 1 is computed in an 8-bit register?
options: It just becomes 100000000 normally.
Overflow - the result requires 9 bits but only 8 are available.
Only the root node.
The computer crashes.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Dijkstra's algorithm”?
options: Finds shortest paths from a source node in a graph with non-negative edge weights.
Algorithmic strategy splitting a problem into independent subproblems, solving recursively then combining.
Best-first graph search using f(n) = g(n) + h(n); guaranteed optimal with an admissible heuristic.
A finite, deterministic, unambiguous sequence of steps that solves a problem in finite time.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Greedy algorithm”?
options: Best-first graph search using f(n) = g(n) + h(n); guaranteed optimal with an admissible heuristic.
Makes the locally optimal choice at each step (e.g., Dijkstra), hoping for a global optimum.
Algorithmic strategy splitting a problem into independent subproblems, solving recursively then combining.
Tries candidate solutions and abandons (backtracks) any that cannot be completed - used in N-queens, sudoku.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Backtracking”?
options: Best-first graph search using f(n) = g(n) + h(n); guaranteed optimal with an admissible heuristic.
Finds shortest paths from a source node in a graph with non-negative edge weights.
Tries candidate solutions and abandons (backtracks) any that cannot be completed - used in N-queens, sudoku.
Makes the locally optimal choice at each step (e.g., Dijkstra), hoping for a global optimum.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Divide and conquer”?
options: Algorithmic strategy splitting a problem into independent subproblems, solving recursively then combining.
Best-first graph search using f(n) = g(n) + h(n); guaranteed optimal with an admissible heuristic.
Finds shortest paths from a source node in a graph with non-negative edge weights.
A finite, deterministic, unambiguous sequence of steps that solves a problem in finite time.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Algorithm”?
options: Best-first graph search using f(n) = g(n) + h(n); guaranteed optimal with an admissible heuristic.
A finite, deterministic, unambiguous sequence of steps that solves a problem in finite time.
Algorithmic strategy splitting a problem into independent subproblems, solving recursively then combining.
Finds shortest paths from a source node in a graph with non-negative edge weights.
